questionText: Town A's description fits the short-term atmospheric condition, which is weather, while Town B shows a long-term, averaged pattern, characteristic of climate.
options: Weather is the study of atmospheric conditions for a short duration of a limited area.
Climate is the study of the average weather conditions observed over a long period of time for a larger area.
Weather is influenced by anyone of its predominant elements i.e., temperature or humidity.
Climate is the collective effect of all its elements.
mnemonic_hint: Weather is your 'Mood' (short-term), Climate is your 'Personality' (long-term).

questionText: The Big Bang Theory considers the following stages in the development of the universe:
options: In the beginning, all matter forming the universe existed in one place in the form of a “tiny ball” (singular atom) with an unimaginably small volume, infinite temperature and infinite density.
At the Big Bang the “tiny ball” exploded violently. This led to a huge expansion. It is now generally accepted that the event of the big bang took place 13.7 billion years before the present.
Within 300,000 years from the Big Bang, temperature dropped to 4,500K (Kelvin) and gave rise to atomic matter. The universe became transparent.
All of the above
sub_topic: Origin and Evolution of the Universe
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'S-E-T': Singularity (tiny ball), Explosion (expansion), and Transparency (atomic matter formation).

questionText: The atmosphere did not exist in its current life-sustaining form when the Earth was formed about 4.6 billion years ago. Instead, it underwent a series of transformational stages due to geological, chemical, and biological processes. These changes were driven by factors like solar radiation, volcanic activity and biological evolution, particularly the emergence of photosynthetic organisms.
options: The first stage of atmospheric evolution was marked by the loss of the primordial atmosphere, which consisted mainly of hydrogen and helium.
The second stage began as Earth cooled. Gases like water vapour, carbon dioxide, nitrogen, and methane were released from the Earth's interior through a process called degassing.
The third stage involved a significant transformation brought about by the emergence of photosynthetic organisms in Earth's oceans.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'P-D-P': Primordial loss, Degassing interior, Photosynthesis oxygenation.

questionText: A habitable planet is one that can sustain life for a significant period; based on our solar system, life requires liquid water, energy and nutrients. A "habitable zone" is the region around a star where planets can receive the perfect amount of heat to maintain liquid water on their surfaces.
options: Earth remains at an optimal distance from the Sun in an almost circular orbit.
Earth has a suitable mass and radius, which allows it to exert a gravitational force strong enough to retain the atmosphere.
Earth’s magnetic field plays a protective role. It shields the surface from harmful high-energy solar radiation.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'G-A-M-E': Gravity (atmosphere), Atmosphere (protection), Magnetic field (radiation shield), Energy (liquid water).

questionText: Earth’s interior structure and composition are characterised by its thermal and physical state. It is divided into several distinct layers based on chemical composition and physical properties.
options: The Sial: It is made up of two words, i.e. Si plus and Al which denote silica and aluminum.
The Sima: A layer situated just below the sial is known as ‘sima’. It is made of basalt material.
The Nife: It is placed beneath the middle layer of sima. Nickel (Ni) and Iron (Fe) are two dominant minerals.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember the layers by their names: SIAL (Silica-Aluminum), SIMA (Silica-Magnesium), and NIFE (Nickel-Ferrous).

questionText: The planets of the solar system are broadly classified into terrestrial and Jovian planets based on their position, composition and physical characteristics.
options: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are terrestrial planets, characterized by their rocky surfaces and proximity to the Sun.
Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are Jovian planets, known for their large sizes, gaseous compositions and location in the outer solar system.
Unlike the terrestrial planets that make up our inner solar system, the Jovian planets do not have solid surfaces.
All of the above
concepts: Compositional differences in solar system bodies
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'My Very Educated Mother' (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) for the rocky inner terrestrial planets.

questionText: The rock cycle is a natural process where igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks constantly change from one type to another over time due to geological forces like weathering, erosion, heat, pressure and tectonic activity.
options: Sedimentary Rocks: Rocks (igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic) of the earth’s surface are exposed to denudational agents and are broken up into various sizes of fragments.
Igneous Rocks: As igneous rocks form out of magma and lava from the interior of the Earth, they are known as primary rocks.
Metamorphic Rocks: The word metamorphic means ‘change of form’. These rocks form under the action of pressure, volume and temperature (PVT) changes.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'SIM': Sedimentary (broken fragments), Igneous (magma/primary), Metamorphic (change of form/PVT).

questionText: Sedimentary Rocks are exposed to denudational agents and are broken up into various sizes of fragments. Such fragments are transported by different exogenous agencies and deposited. These deposits through compaction turn into rocks.
options: Sedimentary Rocks are classified into two types - Clastic and Non-clastic.
Sedimentary rocks showing clastic texture consist of discrete fragments and particles that may be cemented and compacted together.
Some chemical sedimentary rocks have a non-clastic or crystalline texture in which the minerals form a pattern of interlocking crystals.
All of the above
sub_topic: Classification and Formation of Sedimentary Rocks
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'Clastic' as 'Cluttered' (broken fragments) and 'Non-clastic' as 'Neat' (interlocking crystals).

questionText: Diastrophism: All processes that move, elevate or build up portions of the Earth’s crust come under diastrophism.
options: Orogenic processes involving mountain building through severe folding affect long and narrow belts of the Earth’s crust.
Epeirogenic processes involving the uplift or warping of large parts of the Earth’s crust.
Earthquakes involving local relatively minor movements.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'DEO': Diastrophism includes Epeirogenic (large scale) and Orogenic (mountain building) processes.

questionText: Rivers undergo a long journey from their source to mouth and during this journey, they pass through different stages of development — namely the youth, mature and old stages.
options: Youth stage: Streams are few during this stage with poor integration and flow over original slopes showing shallow V-shaped valleys with no floodplains.
Mature stage: During this stage, streams are plentiful with good integration. The valleys are still V shaped but deep; trunk streams are broad enough to have wider floodplains.
Old stage: Smaller tributaries during old age are few with gentle gradients. Streams meander freely over vast floodplains showing natural levees, oxbow lakes, etc.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember YMO: Youth (V-valleys), Mature (Many streams), Old (Oxbows/Meanders).

questionText: All natural earthquakes take place in the lithosphere. Earthquake waves are basically of two types — body waves and surface waves.
options: Primary (P) Waves: Fastest wave and reaches first at the surface.
Secondary (S) Waves: Travels only through the solid state of matter.
Surface/ Long (L) waves: Its velocity is lesser than P and S waves.
All of the above
concepts: State of matter and wave transmission
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'P-S-L': Primary is Prime (fastest), Secondary is Solid-only, and Long (Surface) waves are the Last to arrive.

questionText: The theory of Plate Tectonics explains the large-scale motion of Earth's lithosphere, which is broken into several tectonic plates.
options: At divergent plate boundaries, rising convection currents in the Earth’s mantle bring hot, viscous rock material toward the surface.
Convergent plate boundaries form where convection currents push two tectonic plates toward each other.
Transform boundaries are characterized by plates sliding laterally past one another.
All of the above
sub_topic: Plate Tectonic Theory and Boundary Types
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'D-C-T': Divergent (Divide/Apart), Convergent (Collide/Together), Transform (Twist/Slide).

questionText: On the basis of their geographical location and structure of rocks, the plateaus can be classified as:
options: Intermontane Plateau: The plateau which are bordering the fold mountain range or are partly or fully enclosed within them.
Piedmont Plateau: The plateaus that are situated at the foot of the mountains and are bounded on other sides by a plain or an ocean.
Continental Plateau: These are formed either by an extensive continental uplift or by the spread of horizontal basic lava sheets.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'IPC': Intermontane (Inside mountains), Piedmont (at the Foot/Plain), Continental (Covering vast areas).

questionText: Various evidence supports this theory of continental drift:
options: The Matching of Continents (Jig-Saw-Fit): The shorelines of Africa and South America facing each other have a remarkable and unmistakable match.
Rocks of Same Age Across the Oceans: The radiometric dating methods developed in the recent period have facilitated correlating the rock formation from different continents across the vast ocean.
Placer Deposits: The occurrence of rich placer deposits of gold in the Ghana coast and the absolute absence of source rock in the region is an amazing fact.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'J-R-P': Jig-saw fit, Radiometric rock dating, and Placer deposits are the key proofs for drift.

questionText: The ocean water conceals a considerable variety of landscapes very similar to those on the continents. Ocean basins are broadly divided into four major sub-divisions.
options: Continental shelf
Continental slope
Abyssal plains
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'CSAT' for the four divisions: Continental Shelf, Slope, Abyssal plains, and Trenches.

questionText: Alluvial fans and bajadas are depositional landforms commonly found in arid and semi-arid regions, but they can also occur in other geomorphological contexts.
options: Alluvial fans: When rivers flow down the steep mountain slopes into the valleys they drop their load of coarse - sand and gravels as their sudden decrease in velocity.
A bajada is the convergence, or blending, of many alluvial fans.
Alluvial fans and bajadas are often found in deserts, where flash floods wash alluvium down from nearby hills.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of a 'Fan' spreading out at the base of a mountain, and a 'Bajada' as a 'Bazaar' where many fans meet and merge.

questionText: Slow Movements: Solifluction is a type of slow mass movement that occurs when water-saturated soil or fine-grained debris slowly flows downslope.
options: This process is most common in moist temperate regions.
It occurs especially where surface thawing of frozen ground (such as during seasonal melting) and prolonged rainfall are frequent.
These conditions lead to oversaturation of the upper soil layer, while the lower layers remain impervious, triggering the flow.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'SOLI-FLUX': Soil that is saturated (FLUX) and flows like a slow liquid (SOLI) due to melting ice.

questionText: Exogenic processes are generally called erosional processes which perform three-phase work i.e. erosion, transportation and deposition.
options: Attrition refers to mechanical tear and wear of erosion tools suffered by themselves.
The breakdown of rocks due to pressure exerted by water currents of the rivers and sea waves is termed as Hydraulic action.
Deflation is the process of removing, lifting and blowing away dry and loose particles of sands and dust by winds.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'HAD': Hydraulic (water pressure), Attrition (tools wearing themselves), Deflation (wind lifting dust).

questionText: On the basis of their mode of occurrence, igneous rocks can be classified as extrusive or volcanic rocks and intrusive rocks.
options: Intrusive igneous rocks are created when molten magma cools and solidifies below the Earth’s surface.
Plutonic rocks are a type of intrusive igneous rock that form deep within the Earth’s crust.
Deep-seated intrusive rocks are termed as plutonic rocks and shallow-depth intrusive rocks are termed hypabyssal.
All of the above
concepts: Mode of occurrence of igneous rocks
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'P-H-E': Plutonic (Deep), Hypabyssal (Shallow), Extrusive (Surface).

questionText: Volcanoes are classified on the basis of the nature of eruption and the form developed at the surface.
options: Composite Volcanoes: These volcanoes are characterised by eruptions of cooler and more viscous lavas than basalt.
Caldera: These are the most explosive of the Earth’s volcanoes. They are a large depression formed when a volcano erupts and collapses.
Flood Basalt Provinces: These volcanoes outpour highly fluid lava that flows for long distances.
All of the above
sub_topic: Types of Volcanoes and Volcanic Landforms
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'C-C-F': Composite (Cool/Viscous), Caldera (Collapse/Explosive), Flood (Fluid/Flowing).

questionText: Batholiths are huge masses of solidified magma. They are a large body of magmatic material that cools in the deeper depths of the crust and develops in the form of large domes.
options: They appear on the surface only after the denudational processes remove the overlying materials.
They vary in size; some are as much as several hundred kilometers across and thousands of kilometers thick.
They generally form the core of the major mountains.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of a 'Bath-olith' as a giant bathtub of magma buried deep in the earth's crust that only reveals its 'dome' after the surface is scrubbed away by erosion.

questionText: The Ring of Fire is a roughly 25,000-mile chain of volcanoes and seismically active sites that outline the Pacific Ocean.
options: The Ring of Fire traces the meeting points of many tectonic plates, including the Eurasian, North American, Juan de Fuca, Cocos, Caribbean, Nazca, Antarctic, Indian, Australian, Philippine and other smaller plates.
The plates are constantly sliding past, colliding into, or moving above or below each other.
The tectonic activity along the Ring of Fire also results in about 90% of the world’s earthquakes.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'PACIFIC' as Plates Always Colliding In Frequent Intense Conjunctions.

questionText: The Indian plate includes Peninsular India and the Australian continental portions.
options: The subduction zone along the Himalayas forms the northern plate boundary in the form of continent—continent convergence.
In the east, it extends through the Rakinyoma Mountains of Myanmar towards the island arc along the Java Trench.
Its western margin follows Kirthar Mountain of Pakistan.
All of the above
sub_topic: Plate Tectonics and Indian Plate Boundaries
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'K-H-R' for the Indian plate edges: Kirthar (West), Himalayas (North), and Rakinyoma (East).

questionText: Water vapour present in the air is known as humidity. The actual amount of water vapour present in the atmosphere is known as the absolute humidity.
options: Water vapour is also a variable gas in the atmosphere, which decreases with altitude.
Water vapour also decreases from the equator towards the poles.
It also absorbs parts of the insolation from the sun and preserves the Earth’s radiated heat.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'W-A-R': Water vapour decreases with Altitude, decreases towards poles (latitudinal), and Retains heat.

questionText: The distribution of atmospheric pressure on the surface of the Earth is not uniform. It varies both vertically and horizontally.
options: Air temperature: Air temperature and pressure share an inverse relationship.
The Earth’s rotation: The Earth's rotation creates centrifugal force, causing air to deflect and pressure to decrease.
Presence of water vapour: Air with higher quantity of water vapour has lower pressure and that with lower quantity of water vapour has higher pressure.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'W-A-T': Water vapour, Air temperature, and The Earth's rotation are the three key drivers of pressure.

questionText: All measurements are relative to some standard. Motion is measured relative to a reference frame.
options: Newton's laws of motion are defined with respect to a fixed reference frame.
Newton's laws of motion apply strictly to a fixed, inertial reference frame.
Since the Earth itself is in motion, an apparent force must be introduced to account for the effects of this rotating, non-inertial reference frame.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'FINA': Fixed Inertial, Non-inertial Apparent (force) to distinguish frame types.

questionText: There are four heating processes directly responsible for heating the atmosphere. They are Radiation, Conduction, Convection and Advection.
options: Conduction: When two objects of unequal temperature come in contact with each other, heat energy flows from the warmer object to the cooler object.
Convection: Transfer of heat by movement of a mass or substance from one place to another, generally vertical.
Radiation: It is the process by which solar energy reaches the Earth and the Earth loses energy to outer space.
All of the above
sub_topic: Heating and Cooling of the Atmosphere
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'R-C-C-A': Radiation (Sun), Conduction (Contact), Convection (Currents/Vertical), Advection (Air/Horizontal).

questionText: The changes in the upper air circulation over the Indian landmass are the cause for the sudden outbreak of monsoons in India.
options: Jet streams in the upper air system influence the climate of India.
Jet streams are currents of air high above Earth. They move eastward at altitudes of about 8 to 15 kilometers.
They form where large temperature differences exist in the atmosphere.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'JET' as 'Jumping Earth Temperatures'—where high-altitude temperature contrasts create fast-moving air currents that steer our weather.

questionText: The classification of clouds is based on a combination of form, height and appearance:
options: Cirrostratus (Cs): This resembles a thin white sheet or veil; the sky looks milky and the sun or moon shines through it with a characteristic 'halo'.
Stratocumulus (St-Cu): Grey or whitish, or both grey and whitish, patch, sheet or layer of cloud that almost always has dark parts.
Nimbostratus (Ni-St): Grey cloud layer, often dark, the appearance of which is rendered diffuse by more or less continuously falling rain or snow.
All of the above
concepts: Cloud classification based on form and height
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Cirro' as high/thin, 'Strato' as layered/sheet-like, and 'Nimbo' as rain-bearing.

questionText: The variation of pressure from place to place and from season to season over the earth plays an important role in affecting the weather and climate.
options: In the pressure distribution through isobars, the pressures at all places are reduced to sea level to avoid the effect of altitude on air pressure.
In January, with the south-ward apparent movement of the Sun, the equatorial low pressure belt shifts a little south of the mean equatorial position.
Areas of lowest pressure occur in South America, Southern Africa and Australia.
All of the above
sub_topic: Global Pressure Belts and Atmospheric Circulation
concepts: Reduction of pressure to sea level
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Sun follows the heat': As the Sun moves south, the thermal low-pressure belt follows it south.

questionText: Wind is the movement of air, caused by the uneven heating of the Earth by the sun and the Earth's own rotation.
options: Chinook: It is the name of a hot and dry local wind which moves down the eastern slopes of the Rockies in the U.S.A. and Canada.
Harmattan: It is a hot, dry, dusty wind blowing from the Sahara desert over West Africa into the Gulf of Guinea.
Zonda: It is also called Sondo, winter Foehn. It is a warm, dry wind blowing east of the Andes in Argentina.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'CHZ': Chinook (Rockies), Harmattan (Sahara/West Africa), Zonda (Andes/Argentina).

questionText: The Earth's atmosphere is divided into several layers: the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere.
options: Each layer has distinct temperature characteristics.
The mesosphere is the third layer of the atmosphere which extends up to 80 kms.
The temperature in the mesosphere continuously decreases with increasing height.
All of the above
concepts: Vertical temperature profile of the atmosphere
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'TSMT' (The Sun Makes Temperature) for the order: Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere.

questionText: Winds play an important role in understanding the climatic characteristics of different parts of the world and our surroundings.
options: Planetary winds: The planetary winds blow from high pressure areas to low pressure areas in the same direction throughout the year.
The Easterlies or Trade winds: The Easterlies winds blow from sub-tropical high-pressure areas towards equatorial low-pressure areas.
Polar easterlies: The polar easterlies blow from polar high-pressure regions towards sub-polar low-pressure regions.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'PET': Planetary (all year), Easterlies (Sub-tropical to Equator), Trade (another name for Easterlies).

questionText: Continental margins are underwater edges of continents and consist of three main parts: the continental shelves, continental slope, continental rise and deep-oceanic trenches.
options: Continental Shelf: It is the continental margin which starts from the shoreline and extended upto the continental edge.
Continental Slope: It descends from the edge of the continental shelf down to the deeper ocean floor.
Continental Rise: It lies beyond the continental slope and consists of sediment that has cascaded down the slope.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'S-S-R' for the sequence: Shelf (shallow), Slope (steep), Rise (sediment accumulation).

questionText: Seafloor spreading is a geologic process in which tectonic plates—large slabs of Earth's lithosphere—split apart from each other.
options: Seafloor spreading and other tectonic activity processes are the result of mantle convection.
In some cases, oceanic crust encounters an active plate margin.
Active plate margins are often the site of earthquakes and volcanoes.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'MAP': Mantle convection causes Active margins and Plate movement.

questionText: The temperature-depth profile for the ocean water shows how the temperature decreases with increasing depth.
options: The average surface temperature of ocean water is around 27°C and steadily decreases from the equator toward the poles.
Oceans in the Northern Hemisphere are generally warmer than those in the Southern Hemisphere.
The greater land area in the Northern Hemisphere absorbs more solar radiation, which warms both the land and the adjacent ocean waters.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think 'North is Land-heavy': More land in the North means more heat absorption, making the Northern oceans warmer.

questionText: Ocean currents closely influence the distribution of temperature, pressure, winds and precipitation, which directly or indirectly influence the economy and society of the people.
options: Currents move from warm temperature areas to colder temperature areas and vice versa.
The temperature of a mass of water affects the temperature of the air above it.
The ocean current that moves from the equatorial region to the colder latitudes raises the temperature of the air in the areas into which it moves.
All of the above
sub_topic: Ocean Currents and their Climatic Impact
mnemonic_hint: Think of ocean currents as 'Global Conveyor Belts' that act like a radiator (warm currents) or an air conditioner (cold currents) for the coastal lands they pass.

questionText: Concept of Seafloor spreading: The post-drift studies provided considerable information that was not available at the time Wegener put forth his concept of continental drift.
options: It was realised that all along the mid-oceanic ridges, volcanic eruptions are common and they bring huge amounts of lava to the surface in this area.
The rocks equidistant on either side of the crest of mid-oceanic ridges show remarkable similarities in terms of period of formation, chemical compositions and magnetic properties.
The ocean crust rocks are much younger than the continental rocks.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'V-M-Y': Volcanic ridges, Magnetic symmetry, and Younger crusts prove the seafloor is spreading.

questionText: Ocean currents are the continuous, predictable, directional movement of seawater driven by gravity, wind (Coriolis Effect) and water density.
options: Currents of the Indian Ocean: The pattern of circulation of currents in the Indian Ocean differs from the general pattern of circulation in the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean.
The general pattern of circulation in the southern section of the Indian Ocean is anti-clockwise as is that of other oceans.
In the northern section, there is a clear reversal of currents in winter and summer.
All of the above
sub_topic: Ocean Currents of the Indian Ocean
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Indian Monsoon, Indian Reversal'—unlike the steady Atlantic/Pacific, the Indian Ocean currents dance to the tune of the seasonal monsoon winds.

questionText: The Earth is composed of various kinds of elements. These elements are in solid form in the outer layer of the Earth and in hot and molten form in the interior.
options: Oxygen is the most abundant element in the Earth’s crust by volume, accounting for over 90%.
Silicon is the second most abundant element by volume (0.88%), commonly found as part of silicate minerals.
Aluminium is the third most abundant element by weight in the Earth’s crust, after oxygen and silicon.
All of the above
concepts: Chemical composition of the Earth's crust
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'OSI-AL' (Oxygen, Silicon, Aluminium) to recall the top three most abundant elements in the Earth's crust by weight.

questionText: Soil is a thin layer made up of broken rock particles, organic matter, water and air that covers most of the land.
options: Soil is essential for life on Earth and is one of our most valuable natural resources.
All soils are made from four main parts: air, water, organic matter and minerals.
Dark-coloured soils get their colour from a high content of organic matter.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'MAAW' for soil components: Minerals, Air, Air (Water), and Water (Organic matter).

questionText: The primary igneous and secondary sedimentary rocks may change their physical and chemical characteristics and form due to the huge pressure and heat.
options: Metamorphism makes the rocks go through the process of re-crystallization which results in the transformation of the Protolith into harder and denser rock.
Metamorphic rocks are denser and harder than the original parent rock.
They may contain well developed foliated or lineated structures.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'M-H-D': Metamorphism makes rocks Harder and Denser.

questionText: Any limestone or dolomitic region showing typical landforms produced by the action of groundwater through the processes of solution and deposition is called Karst topography.
options: The karst topography is characterised by erosional and depositional landforms.
Karst regions have a bleak landscape, occasionally broken by precipitous slopes.
Processes related to the dissolution of soluble rocks, such as limestone and gypsum, by water are known as karst processes.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'KARST' as 'K-hemical Action, Rocks Soluble, Terrain' to remember the process of limestone dissolution.

questionText: Sand dunes: A Landform is created by the movement of sand by wind. The dunes are like small mountains, ridges or hills.
options: Barchan: They are crescent (half-moon) or arc-shaped, appear convex in shape and are primarily formed by wind from one direction.
Transverse dunes: These dunes are asymmetrical in shape and form where light to moderate winds blow from a constant direction.
Seif or longitudinal dunes: They are long, narrow ridges that are parallel to the direction of prevailing winds.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'B-C' (Barchan-Crescent) and 'S-P' (Seif-Parallel) to distinguish dune shapes and their wind alignment.

questionText: Depositional Landforms: Many depositional forms develop within the limestone caves.
options: Stalactites hang as icicles of different diameters.
Stalagmites rise up from the floor of the caves.
Stalagmites may take the shape of a column, a disc, with either a smooth, rounded bulging end or a miniature crater-like depression.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Stalactites hold 'tight' to the ceiling, while Stalagmites 'might' reach the top.

questionText: The Earth's mantle, which lies between the crust and the core, is primarily divided into two main layers: the upper mantle and the lower mantle.
options: The boundary that separates these two layers is known as the Repetti Discontinuity.
Upper Mantle: Though mostly solid, parts of the upper mantle are ductile (more malleable), which plays a crucial role in tectonic activity.
Transition Zone: It is located between 410 km and 660 km depth, this zone acts as a boundary within the mantle.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember the order of discontinuities with 'Conrad, Mohorovicic, Repetti, Gutenberg, Lehmann' (CMRGL) - 'Can My Red Goat Like Grass?'

questionText: Deposition develops a floodplain just as erosion makes valleys. A floodplain is a major landform of river deposition.
options: The flood deposits of spilled waters carry relatively finer materials like silt and clay.
Natural levees are found along the banks of large rivers. They are low, linear and parallel ridges of coarse deposits along the banks of rivers.
Point bars are also known as meander bars. They are found on the concave side of meanders of large rivers.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'L-C-P': Levees are Coarse, Point bars are on the Concave side, and Plains are made of fine Silt.

questionText: Delta is a triangular feature with its apex pointing up stream and has a fan shaped area of fine alluvium.
options: There should be active lateral and vertical erosion in the upper course of the river to provide large amounts of sediments.
Shallow sea water adjoining the delta.
Tideless and sheltered coast.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'SST': Sediment supply, Shallow sea, and Tideless coast are the three pillars of a delta's birth.

questionText: Masses of ice moving as sheets over the land or as linear flows down the slopes of mountains in broad trough-like valleys (mountain and valley glaciers) are called glaciers.
options: Aretes are saw-toothed ridges in which there are multiple ridges in series and rows and they divide two cirques.
Cols are shallow passes between two high points of the mountain.
Horn is pyramid shaped mountain peaks which is formed by erosion on three sides by 3-4 cirques on each side of the peak.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: ACH: Aretes (saw-toothed), Cols (passes), Horns (pyramid peaks) are the glacial trio.

questionText: Fold Mountains: Folded mountains are formed due to folding of crustal rocks by compressive forces generated by endogenetic forces coming from within the earth.
options: These are the highest and most extensive mountains of the world and are found in all the continents.
Block Mountains: Block mountains are the result of faulting caused by tensile and compressive forces motored by endogenetic forces coming from within the earth.
Block mountains represent the upstanding parts of the ground between two faults or on either side of a rift valley or a graben.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Fold is for compression (like a rug), Block is for faulting (like a broken block).

questionText: Mountains are significant relief features of the second order on the Earth’s surface. A mountain may have several forms.
options: Residual mountains: They are formed through the prolonged erosion of elevated landforms, leaving behind resistant remnants.
Volcanic Mountains: When tectonic plates move about, volcanoes are formed and when volcanoes erupt, mountains are formed in turn.
Dome mountains: They are formed when large globs of magma float up from beneath the crust and push up surface rocks, creating a rounded swelling in the crust.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'RVD': Residual (eroded), Volcanic (erupted), Dome (pushed up).

questionText: In 1912, German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed the Continental Drift Theory, offering a comprehensive explanation for the distribution of continents and oceans.
options: According to Wegener, all present-day continents were once part of a single massive landmass called Pangaea.
Wegener suggested that around 200 million years ago, Pangaea began to break apart.
To support his theory, Wegener presented multiple lines of evidence, including matching geological structures, fossil records and climatic similarities across continents.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Pangaea' as the 'Pan-Earth' (all-earth) supercontinent that drifted apart like puzzle pieces.

questionText: Minerals are naturally occurring inorganic substances with definite chemical compositions and physical properties.
options: Amphibole: Aluminium, calcium, silica, iron, magnesium are the major elements of amphiboles.
Quartz: It is one of the most important components of sand and granite. It consists of silica.
Feldspar: Silicon and oxygen are common elements in all types of feldspar.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'F-Q-A' (Feldspar, Quartz, Amphibole) as the 'Big Three' rock-formers: Feldspar is the most abundant, Quartz is pure silica, and Amphibole is the complex iron-magnesium mix.

questionText: Winds are the most widespread geomorphic agents in the deserts, arid and semi-arid regions.
options: Wind erosion is effective only up to 180 cm above the ground surface.
Loess: It is primarily located close to the desert floor or crust and is a feature made by deposition.
Yardangs: These are elongated ridges formed by wind oriented with the prevailing winds.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Y-A-R' for Yardangs: Y-shaped ridges aligned with the prevailing winds.

questionText: Landslides: These are relatively rapid and perceptible movements. The materials involved are relatively dry.
options: The size and shape of the detached mass depend on the nature of discontinuities in the rock, the degree of weathering and the steepness of the slope.
Landslides are more frequent in the Himalayan region when compared with the Western Ghats.
Topography plays a crucial role in landslide formation.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'H-W-S' for landslides: Himalayas (high frequency), Weathering (rock decay), and Slope (steepness).

questionText: Pediments: Landscape evolution in deserts is primarily concerned with the formation and extension of pediments.
options: These are gently sloping terrains found at the foot of the mountains over a solid rock base formed due to abrasion.
They are the junction that occurs between the zone of a steep erosional slope and the depositional lowlands.
Such rocky floors form through the erosion of the mountain front through a combination of lateral erosion by streams and sheet flooding.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of a PEDIMENT as a 'PED-I-MENT' (Pedal/Foot-Mountain-Element): The gentle foot-slope element formed by mountain erosion.

questionText: A tectonic plate (also called a lithospheric plate) is a massive, irregularly-shaped slab of solid rock, generally composed of both continental and oceanic lithosphere.
options: Plates move horizontally over the asthenosphere as rigid units.
The theory of plate tectonics proposes that the Earth’s lithosphere is divided into seven major and some minor plates.
Scotia Plate: Between the South American Plate and the Antarctic Plate.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'S-A-A' for the Scotia Plate: Scotia is between South American and Antarctic plates.

questionText: The magma is heavily charged with gases such as carbon dioxide, sulphurated hydrogen and small proportions of nitrogen, chlorine and other volatile substances.
options: The gases and vapour increase the mobility and explosiveness of the lavas which are emitted through the orifice or vent of a volcano during a volcanic eruption.
Basic lavas: These are the hottest lavas and are highly fluid.
Acid lavas: These lavas are highly viscous with a high melting point.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'B-H-F' for Basic (Hottest, Fluid) and 'A-V-H' for Acid (Viscous, High melting point).

questionText: Soil colour is the physical property of soil. It varies widely depending on the nature of parent material, organic matter content, climate, drainage conditions and aeration.
options: The red colour of a soil is due to the presence of iron compounds or manganese dioxides.
Well-developed red coloured soil has good drainage and aeration.
Well-drained yellow soils have small amounts of organic matter and other colouring material such as iron oxides.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'IRON-RED': Iron oxides give the red hue, while yellow indicates hydration or lower iron concentration.

questionText: Latitude: It is the angular distance of a point on the Earth’s surface, measured in degrees from the centre of the Earth.
options: It is parallel to a line, the equator, which lies midway between the poles.
All the parallels or latitudes except the equator go on becoming smaller towards the poles.
Latitudes always run in the east-west direction.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Lats are Flats' (horizontal lines) and 'Longs are Long' (vertical lines from pole to pole).

questionText: The atmosphere consists of different layers with varying density and temperature.
options: The stratosphere is found above the tropopause and extends up to a height of 50 km.
One important feature of the stratosphere is that it contains the ozone layer.
Because of its stability and low turbulence, this layer is ideal for certain types of aircraft and scientific observations.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Ozone in the Stratosphere' (O-S) as the 'Safe' layer for jets due to low turbulence.

questionText: As the winter season transforms into the spring season, the temperature rises, giving rise to thunderstorms, which are hazardous.
options: Thunderstorms have been defined as storms produced by a cumulonimbus cloud and are always accompanied by intense lightning and thunder.
It is also characterised by intense updraft of rising warm air, which causes the clouds to grow bigger and rise to greater height.
Severe storms, dust clouds and volcanic eruptions can also generate lightning.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'C-U-L': Cumulonimbus clouds, Updrafts, and Lightning are the three pillars of a thunderstorm.

questionText: Relief features such as mountains, plateaus and plains control the temperature by way of modifying its distribution.
options: Mountains act as barriers against the movement of winds.
As we move upwards from sea level, we experience a gradual decrease in temperature.
The air at lower elevations is warmer than that of higher elevations because it is closer to the heated surface of the Earth.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'ALT-itude': As you go ALT-up, the heat goes ALT-down.

questionText: Heat budget of the Earth:
options: The insolation is made up of energy transmitted directly through the atmosphere and scattered energy.
The insolation received by the Earth is in short waves and heats up its surface.
The Earth after being heated itself becomes a radiating body and it radiates energy to the atmosphere in long wave form.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Short Sun, Long Land': Solar energy arrives in short waves, but the Earth cools down by emitting long waves.

questionText: The spatial distribution of precipitation is not uniform all over the world.
options: In general, as we proceed from the equator towards the poles, rainfall goes on decreasing steadily.
The coastal areas of the world receive greater amounts of rainfall than the interior of the continents.
The equatorial regions and the western parts of temperate lands receive precipitation throughout the year.
All of the above
sub_topic: World Climatic Patterns and Precipitation Distribution
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'E-C-W': Equatorial (high), Coastal (high), Western-temperate (high) are the wet zones of the world.

questionText: Evaporation is a process by which water is transformed from liquid to gaseous state. Heat is the main cause for evaporation.
options: The transformation of water vapour into water is called condensation.
Condensation is caused by the loss of heat.
Dew is formed when the moisture is deposited in the form of water droplets on cooler surfaces of solid objects.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'E-G-C-L': Evaporation Gains heat (liquid to gas), Condensation Loses heat (gas to liquid).

questionText: Inversion of Temperature:
options: Long winter nights, clear sky, dry air and absence of winds lead to quick radiation of heat from the Earth’s surface.
The phenomenon of inversion of temperature is especially observed in intermontane valleys because during winters, the mountain slopes cool very rapidly.
Sometimes the temperature falls below the freezing point in the valleys leading to the occurrence of frost.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'C-C-D-A' for ideal inversion: Clear skies, Calm winds, Dry air, and Absence of clouds.

questionText: An air mass is an extensive portion of the atmosphere having uniform characteristics of temperature, pressure and moisture which are relatively homogeneous horizontally.
options: An air mass develops when the air over a vast and relatively uniform land or ocean surface remains stationary for a long time.
Arctic air masses, designated by the letter "A", originate over the Arctic or Antarctic regions and therefore are very cold.
Tropical air masses, designated by the letter "T", originate over the lower latitudes of both land and sea and therefore are warm/hot.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'A' for Arctic (Always cold) and 'T' for Tropical (Toasty/Hot).

questionText: Jet streams are relatively narrow bands of strong wind in the upper levels of the atmosphere, typically occurring around 30,000 feet (9,100 meters) in elevation.
options: Within jet streams, the winds blow from west to east, but the band often shifts north and south.
Since these hot and cold air boundaries are most pronounced in winter, jet streams are the strongest during both the northern and southern hemisphere winters.
Jet streams can transport aerosols such as smoke and gases such as ozone, very long distances.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'JET': J-et streams (West to East), E-levation (High), T-ransport (Aerosols/Gases).

questionText: Typical cyclones are an elliptical arrangement of isobars having low pressure at the centre with a convergence of winds within them.
options: Tropical cyclones are formed along the zone of confluence of north-east and south-east trade winds.
There are no clear warm and cold fronts as temperature seldom differs in the Inter Tropical Convergence Zone.
The arrangement of isobars is almost circular.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of ITCZ as a 'Warm Blanket' where fronts can't form because the temperature is uniformly hot.

questionText: Orographic or Relief Rainfall:
options: It is formed where air rises and cools because of a topographic barrier.
When their temperature falls below the dew point, clouds are formed.
A famous example of orographic rainfall is Cherrapunji on the southern margin of the Khasi Hills in Meghalaya India.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'ORO' as 'OR-o-graphic' (OR-ographic) where the mountain acts as an 'OR' (barrier) forcing air to rise.

questionText: The ocean currents are the large masses of surface water that circulate in regular patterns around the oceans.
options: Warm currents: These currents flow from equatorial regions towards the Polar Regions and hence have a higher surface temperature.
Cold currents: These currents flow from Polar Regions towards the equator and have a lower surface temperature.
Currents in the Pacific Ocean: Warm Currents are; North Equatorial Current, South Equatorial Current, Counter Equatorial Current, Kuroshio System, East Australia Current, and North Pacific Drift.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'W-E-P' (Warm-Equator-Pole) for warm currents and 'C-P-E' (Cold-Pole-Equator) for cold currents.

questionText: Tides: The periodical rise and fall of the water level in oceans and sea, once or twice a day, due to the gravitational pull of the sun and the moon, is called a tide.
options: The three major forces that cause the occurrence of tides are Moon's gravitational pull, Sun's gravitational pull, and Centrifugal force.
Neap Tides: After seven days of spring tides the sun and the moon form a 90-degree angle between each other.
Apogee: When the moon's orbit is farthest from the Earth, it is called apogee.
All of the above
concepts: Lunar and Solar influence on Earth
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'S-M-C' for the three forces: Sun, Moon, and Centrifugal force.

questionText: Water vapour is water in gaseous form instead of liquid form. It is also the most important gas in the atmosphere.
options: The Hydrosphere is the source of atmospheric water vapour.
Water vapour is also a variable gas in the atmosphere, which decreases with altitude.
The existence of water vapour also affects the atmospheric pressure.
All of the above
concepts: Role of water vapour in atmospheric stability and pressure
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'W-A-V-E': Water vapour is Atmospheric, Variable, and affects Equilibrium (pressure).

questionText: The Baltic Sea is a marginal sea of the Atlantic Ocean, located in Northern Europe.
options: It is considered the youngest sea on Earth, having formed around 10,000 to 15,000 years ago.
The Dead Sea, also known as the Salt Sea, is a saline lake situated in Southwestern Asia.
The Dead Sea is renowned for being one of the saltiest water bodies on Earth.
All of the above
sub_topic: World Geography - Major Seas and Lakes
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Baltic is Baby' (youngest) and 'Dead is Dense' (salty/buoyant).

questionText: The temperature-depth profile for the ocean water shows how the temperature decreases with increasing depth.
options: The profile shows a boundary region between the surface waters of the ocean and the deeper layers.
The boundary usually begins around 100 - 400 m below the sea surface and extends several hundred metres downward.
About 90 per cent of the total volume of water is found below the thermocline in the deep ocean.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'Thermo-cline' as a 'Thermal Cliff'—a steep drop-off starting just below the surface that separates the warm top from the massive cold deep.

questionText: Seamount: It is a mountain with pointed summits, rising from the seafloor that does not reach the surface of the ocean.
options: Seamounts are volcanic in origin.
Submarine Canyon: These are deep valleys, some comparable to the Grand Canyon of the Colorado River.
Atoll: These are low islands found in the tropical oceans consisting of coral reefs surrounding a central depression.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'S-V-A': Seamounts are Volcanic, Canyons are deep Valleys, and Atolls are circular coral islands.

questionText: The temperature of the surface water of the oceans varies in much the same way as that of the land surface.
options: Latitude: The temperature of surface water decreases from the equator towards the poles because the amount of insolation decreases poleward.
Prevailing wind: The winds blowing from the land towards the oceans drive warm surface water away from the coast.
Ocean currents: Warm ocean currents raise the temperature in cold areas while the cold currents decrease the temperature in warm ocean areas.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'L-W-C': Latitude (sun), Winds (push), and Currents (flow) all dictate how ocean water glows (warms).

questionText: An ocean gyre is a large system of circular ocean currents formed by global wind patterns and forces created by Earth’s rotation.
options: The movement of the world’s major ocean gyres helps drive the “ocean conveyor belt.”
Three forces cause the circulation of a gyre: global wind patterns, Earth’s rotation and Earth’s landmasses.
Earth’s rotation deflects, or changes the direction of, these wind-driven currents.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'W-R-L' for Gyre formation: Winds, Rotation (Coriolis), and Landmasses.

questionText: All waters in nature, whether rainwater or ocean water, contain dissolved mineral salts.
options: Salinity is the term used to define the total content of dissolved salts in seawater.
Increasing the salinity of seawater increases the density of the ocean water.
Higher temperatures generally decrease the density of ocean water.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Salty-Heavy, Hot-Light': High salinity adds mass (density), while high heat makes molecules spread out (lower density).

questionText: Deserts are regions of scanty rainfall which may be hot like the hot deserts of the Saharan type or cold deserts like ladakh.
options: The major hot deserts of the world are located on the western coasts of continents between latitudes 15° and 30°N and S.
The hot deserts lie astride the Horse Latitudes or the Sub-Tropical High Pressure Belts.
On the western coasts of continents, the presence of cold ocean currents cools the moist air moving in from the sea.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'W-H-C': Western coasts, Horse latitudes, and Cold currents create the world's hot deserts.

questionText: The Siberian climate is an example of a severe continental climate and is characterized by very cold winters, relatively warm summers and extreme temperature variations between seasons.
options: The continents in the Southern Hemisphere, such as South America and Africa, become much narrower as they extend towards the poles.
The Southern Hemisphere has vast oceanic expanses, with fewer large landmasses interrupting them.
The Siberian type of climate is absent in the Southern Hemisphere primarily because the southern continents are narrow at high latitudes.
All of the above
concepts: Influence of landmass size on temperature range
mnemonic_hint: Think 'Siberia needs land to freeze': No wide land at high southern latitudes means no Siberian climate there.

questionText: Coniferous forests, also known as taiga or boreal forests, are typically found in high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere.
options: These forests are dominated by a few species of cone-bearing trees such as pine, spruce and fir.
Equatorial rainforests have high biodiversity and are dense with multilayered vegetation.
Unlike deciduous trees, which shed all their leaves annually in autumn and grow new ones in spring, coniferous trees retain their needle-like leaves for several years.
All of the above
concepts: Adaptation of flora to cold climates
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Taiga' as 'T-A-I-G-A' (Trees Always In Green Array) to recall they are evergreen.

questionText: The names Ladang, Taungya, Tamrai, and Humah are primarily associated with shifting cultivation practices in Southeast Asia.
options: These terms refer to traditional agricultural systems where forest land is cleared using slash-and-burn methods.
Ladang in Malaysia and Humah in Java and Taungya refer to a system in Myanmar that also integrates tree planting with crop cultivation.
Tamrai is used in Thailand for similar upland shifting practices.
All of the above
sub_topic: Types of Agriculture and Shifting Cultivation
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'L-T-T-H' for Southeast Asia: Ladang (Malaysia), Taungya (Myanmar), Tamrai (Thailand), and Humah (Java/Indonesia).

questionText: A steppe is a dry, grassy plain. Steppes occur in temperate climates, which lie between the tropics and polar regions.
options: These grasslands lie in the Westerly wind belt, which influences their general weather patterns.
While the Steppe climate in the Northern Hemisphere experience extreme seasonal variations, this is not true for the Southern Hemisphere.
The Steppe climate receives less rainfall than the tropical savanna, which significantly affects the type of vegetation found in each region.
All of the above
concepts: Influence of planetary winds on regional climate
mnemonic_hint: Think of STEPPE as 'STEEP' temperature changes in the North, and 'Westerly' winds blowing across the plains.

questionText: Panama Canal: It connects the Atlantic Ocean in the east to the Pacific Ocean in the west.
options: It has been constructed across the Panama Isthmus between Panama City and Colon by the United States of America (USA) government.
Suez Canal: The Suez Canal in Egypt connects the Mediterranean with the Red Sea and is a dividing line between Africa and Asia.
Dardanelles Strait: It is a narrow waterway forming the border between Asian Turkey and European Turkey.
All of the above
sub_topic: Major Canals and Straits of the World
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'Suez-Red-Med' (Suez connects Red Sea and Mediterranean) and 'Panama-Pacific-Atlantic' (Panama links the two major oceans).

questionText: Uranium and thorium are naturally occurring, radioactive heavy metals with unusual properties.
options: Thorium is much more abundant than uranium in rocks from the Earth's crust.
Uranium and thorium are both silvery white-grey radioactive metals that corrode to black oxide in air.
The uranium isotope uranium-235 is the only naturally occurring fissile material.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think 'U-235 is the only natural fissile star' (U-235 is the only naturally occurring fissile isotope).

questionText: The highest level of decision makers or policy makers perform quinary activities.
options: Quinary activities are services that focus on the creation, re-arrangement and interpretation of new and existing ideas.
Medical services for overseas patients in India involves providing healthcare services such as surgeries, diagnostics and treatments to international patients.
A tourist guide, though part of the service sector, does not fall under the quinary category.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'Quinary' as 'Queen-ary'—the highest level of decision-makers (like Queens/Leaders) who set the policy.

questionText: Most demographic concepts are expressed as rates or ratios – they involve two numbers.
options: The fertility rate refers to the number of live births per 1000 women in the child-bearing age group.
The infant mortality rate is the number of deaths of babies before the age of one year per 1000 live births.
The sex ratio refers to the number of females per 1000 males in a given area at a specified time period.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'F-I-S' (Fertility, Infant, Sex): Fertility is per 1000 women, Infant is per 1000 births, and Sex is per 1000 males.

questionText: South Africa is by far the largest producer of platinum in the world.
options: China has the largest share of the world’s reserve of Rare Earth Elements (REEs).
The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is the world's largest producer of cobalt.
India has the world’s fifth-largest rare earth reserves.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'P-C-R': Platinum (South Africa), Cobalt (DRC), Rare Earths (China).

questionText: Population migration refers to the movement of people from one geographical location to another, either within a country (internal migration) or across national borders (international migration).
options: Frequent natural disasters like floods and droughts are examples of push factors for migration.
Availability of better employment opportunities in cities is not a push factor but a pull factor.
Political instability, civil wars, ethnic conflicts and other forms of armed violence are strong push factors.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of PUSH as 'Pushed away' by problems (disasters, war) and PULL as 'Pulled towards' potential (jobs, better life).

questionText: Essequibo is a disputed region that is administered and controlled by Guyana.
options: Abyei is a disputed region between Sudan and South Sudan.
Tigray is a region in northern Ethiopia.
Socotra is an island in the Arabian Sea and is part of Yemen.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'G-E-A-T-S': Guyana-Essequibo, Abyei-Sudan, Tigray-Ethiopia, Socotra-Yemen.

questionText: Footloose industry is a general term for an industry that can be placed and located at any location without effect from factors of production such as resources, land, labour, and capital.
options: These industries produce their products in small numbers and they do not require a large labour force.
Footloose industries produce in relatively small quantities, employing smaller workforces and are considered to be more efficient from an ecological point of view.
Diamonds, computer chips and mobile manufacturing are some examples of footloose industries.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of a 'Footloose' person who can travel anywhere without being tied down by heavy baggage (resources/labor).

questionText: Phnom Penh is the capital of Cambodia and is located around 11.5° N latitude.
options: Bangkok is the capital of Thailand and is situated at around 13.7° N latitude.
Vientiane is the capital of Laos and is located at approximately 17.9° N latitude.
Hanoi is the capital of Vietnam and lies at around 21.0° N latitude.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of the 'V' in Vientiane (Laos) being higher up the map than the 'B' in Bangkok (Thailand) and 'P' in Phnom Penh (Cambodia).

questionText: Eastern Maritime Corridor (EMC): The Chennai-Vladivostok Sea Route, also known as the EMC, connects South India with Russia’s Far East region.
options: The EMC passes through key waterways, including the Sea of Japan, East China Sea, South China Sea, Malacca Straits, Andaman Sea and the Bay of Bengal.
Ports along the route include Dalian, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Ho Chi Minh City, Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Bangkok, Dhaka, Colombo and Chennai.
According to the recent data, a significant increase in cargo volumes on the EMC, with coal shipments rising by 87 per cent and crude oil transport growing by 48 per cent year-on-year in FY 2024–25.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think of 'EMC' as 'East-Maritime-Connection' linking the Chennai heat to the Vladivostok cold.

questionText: Danube River: It is the second-longest river of the European continent, after the Volga River.
options: Brasília, the capital of Brazil, is an inland city and is not located on the Rio de la Plata.
Yangtze River: It is the world’s third-longest river after the Nile and Amazon Rivers.
Seine River: It is France’s second-longest river after the Loire.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'V-D' for Europe (Volga-Danube) and 'N-A-Y' for the world (Nile-Amazon-Yangtze).

questionText: Cool Temperate Western Margin Climate (British-type climate): The cool temperate western margins are under the permanent influence of the Westerlies all round the year.
options: There is so much oceanic influence on both the temperature and the precipitation that the climate is also referred to as the North-West European Maritime Climate.
The natural vegetation of this climatic type is deciduous forest.
The trees shed their leaves in the cold season.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Think 'B-O-D': British climate is Oceanic, and Deciduous trees shed leaves to survive the cold.

questionText: Among the world's landlocked countries, Kazakhstan is the largest, covering an area of approximately 2,724,900 square kilometers.
options: It is followed by Mongolia, with an area of about 1,564,116 sq km.
Chad, which spans 1,284,000 sq km.
Other notable large landlocked nations include Niger (1,267,000 sq km), Mali (1,240,192 sq km) and Ethiopia (1,104,300 sq km).
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'K-M-C-N-M-E' for the largest landlocked countries: Kazakhstan, Mongolia, Chad, Niger, Mali, Ethiopia.

questionText: The Mediterranean climate (classified as Cs in the Koppen system) is typically found along the western coasts of continents in the subtropical latitudes.
options: This climate type experiences hot, dry summers and mild, rainy winters.
During summer, these regions fall under the influence of subtropical high-pressure systems, which suppress rainfall.
While during winter, the westerlies shift equatorward and bring cyclonic rainfall.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'MED-WET': Mediterranean regions have Dry summers and Wet winters.

questionText: Horn of Africa: It is the easternmost projection of the African continent into the Arabian Sea.
options: This region is notable for its diverse topography, ranging from the highlands of the Ethiopian Plateau to the Ogaden desert.
Its coastline is washed by the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, located between Djibouti and Yemen, separates the Horn of Africa from the Arabian Peninsula.
All of the above
mnemonic_hint: Remember 'SEED' for the Horn of Africa: Somalia, Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Djibouti.
